solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Summon British judge when denied right (6)

indicators.note: a word denied something has to go without it, so RECKON loses its R

blocks.note: B = British
RECKON (judge, estimate) without R for right

explanation.surface: A British court sends for someone, and the judge has somehow lost the right to do it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a person on the bench, but here it is the verb: to reckon is to judge or estimate.
explanation.definitionFit: To beckon someone is to signal them to come, which is to summon them.

clue.text: Produce boring article, but with nothing out of place (5,5)

indicators.note: the O is in the wrong word: it leaves BORING and turns up in BUT

blocks.note: BORING with its O taken out
the indefinite article
the word itself
O = nothing (zero), moved into BUT to make BOUT

explanation.surface: Someone is told to write a dull piece, but to keep every word tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue writes out BORING A BUT almost as it stands; the only change is that the O (nothing) has moved one word along.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to produce a result is to cause it to happen, as in producing a change of heart.

clue.text: Work is authorised to repeated cheers (7)

blocks.note: if you are authorised to do something, you can
ta is British slang for thanks, and so is 'cheers'; repeated gives TA TA

explanation.surface: Someone is officially allowed to receive round after round of applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' here is the British thank-you, not applause: ta means thanks. 'Work' is a musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantata is a musical composition for voices, one kind of work.

clue.text: Wilson’s educational project, maybe Heath unveiled (5)

blocks.note: the Open University, set up under Prime Minister Harold Wilson
Edward 'Ted' Heath, Wilson's rival and successor as Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Two British Prime Ministers of the 1960s and 70s and one of their pet projects.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open University is Britain's distance-learning university, founded by Harold Wilson's government; Ted Heath followed him as Prime Minister. 'Maybe' says Heath is just one example of a Ted.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone outed has had a secret about them unveiled in public.

clue.text: Service area cut down extensively (8)

blocks.note: a Mass is a church service
an acre is a unit of area

explanation.surface: A motorway service area has been drastically trimmed back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service area' reads as one thing, the stop on a motorway, but it splits into a church service and a measure of land.
explanation.definitionFit: To massacre is to kill in large numbers, to cut people down extensively.

clue.text: Ditch at first hidden I see now (3)

indicators.note: the first letter is hidden from view, so it drops out

blocks.note: a sunken boundary ditch on a country estate, named for the surprise of finding it

explanation.surface: A trench that was invisible at first suddenly becomes visible.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a feature of English country estates: a ditch with a wall on one side, keeping livestock out without a fence in the view.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Aha' is what you say when you finally see it, meaning 'I see now'.

clue.text: Wind resistance cut by fastening sail (9)

indicators.note: PIN slices into the middle of SNAKER

blocks.note: to wind, as a road does, is to snake
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
a pin is a fastening; it goes in after the first S of SNAKER

explanation.surface: Wind resistance against a sail is reduced by how the sail is fastened.
explanation.walkthrough: With a sail in the clue, 'wind' wants to be the breeze; it is the verb (rhymes with 'find'), to twist like a snake.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinnaker is the large, balloon-shaped sail flown at the front of a yacht.

clue.text: Very leisurely climbing last month, bagging modest peak (7)

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading upwards, so DEC becomes CED
to bag is to capture, so CED takes HILL inside it

blocks.note: DEC is the calendar abbreviation for December, the last month; climbing turns it into CED
a hill is a modest peak; it sits between the C and the ED

explanation.surface: A walker in December completes a small summit, climbing slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bagging' is hillwalkers' slang for climbing a summit to tick it off a list, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Chilled, in slang, means very relaxed and laid-back.

clue.text: Get out of your office? (4)

blocks.note: the surface says leave; the setter means obtain from
not a building but an office in the sense of a post or job

explanation.surface: An order, or a plea, to leave your workplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get out' reads as leave; it means obtain, and the office is your job: what you get out of it is what you earn.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn is to get money in return for your work.

clue.text: Flattest part of pitch, until tackle (6,2,2)

blocks.note: the square is the closely mown central area of a cricket field where the pitches are prepared
up to = until

explanation.surface: A player tackles someone right up to the smoothest part of the football pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tackle' and 'pitch' point to football, but the square belongs to cricket: the prepared, flat strip in the middle of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: To square up to a problem or person is to confront it, to tackle it.

clue.text: Where louse develops, surely? (5)

blocks.note: a louse starts life inside its egg, a nit; two words run together
London slang contracting 'isn't it?', tagged on to seek agreement

explanation.surface: A mock question about where lice come from, answered with a knowing 'surely?'.
explanation.walkthrough: A nit is the egg of a louse. Innit, short for 'isn't it', is London street slang tagged on the end of a sentence, as 'surely?' can be.
explanation.definitionFit: Innit? and surely? both ask the listener to agree with what was just said.

clue.text: Heat from Iraqi fuel supply (9)

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple: the letters are bent into a new shape

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Heat produced by oil from Iraq.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is not the noun here but the adverb from supple ('SUP-lee'). 'Heat' is a sporting heat, not warmth.
explanation.definitionFit: A heat is a preliminary round in a race, a qualifier for the final.

clue.text: Good new genetic material collected by intelligent race (5,8)

indicators.note: NDNA is gathered inside RATIONAL

blocks.note: G = good
rational = able to reason
N = new
the molecule that carries genes; N + DNA goes into RATIONAL after its RA

explanation.surface: A clever breed of horse is being bred from good new genes.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National is Britain's most famous steeplechase, run each spring at Aintree near Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Britain's best-known steeplechase is one instance of a race.

clue.text: Impractical doctor elicits aid (10)

indicators.note: as a verb, to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters are altered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: An unrealistic doctor manages to get help from others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as a person described as impractical; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone idealistic pursues ideals over what is achievable, which is impractical.

clue.text: Words misinterpreted on say, BA opening Macron’s case (10)

indicators.note: BA is given as an example of a degree
ON DEGREE opens up the middle of Macron's case
a word's case is its outside, its first and last letters

blocks.note: outer letters of MACRON
the word itself
a BA (Bachelor of Arts) is a degree; ON DEGREE goes inside M…N

explanation.surface: A remark by President Macron about a British university degree gets misread.
explanation.walkthrough: A mondegreen is a misheard phrase, named after 'laid him on the green' heard as 'Lady Mondegreen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mondegreen is a set of words misheard and so misinterpreted, usually a song lyric.

clue.text: Utter profanity my head regularly bleeps out (9)

indicators.note: take every other letter of MY HEAD: M, H, A
out of order, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: alternate letters of MY HEAD
anagram fodder, with MHA

explanation.surface: A broadcaster's censor bleeps out the swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a TV bleep over a swear word, which is exactly what blaspheming would earn.
explanation.definitionFit: To blaspheme is to utter profanity, speaking irreverently about the sacred.

clue.text: Pay for each item European put in pastry box (5,4)

indicators.note: E is placed inside PIE CRATE

blocks.note: a pie is pastry
a crate is a box
E = European, put in PIE CRATE just after the C

explanation.surface: Each European item is packed into a box of pastries.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to 'each item', which reads as part of the surface's packing instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece rate is a wage paid per item produced rather than per hour.

clue.text: Dear boy turned queer I think in the end (5)

indicators.note: the whole string is turned round
take only the end letter of THINK

blocks.note: queer in its old sense of strange = odd
the word itself
last letter of THINK; all three chunks are then turned round

explanation.surface: Someone says a young man has become strange, they think, in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queer' is used in its older sense of odd or strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Kiddo is an affectionate form of address to a young person, like 'dear boy'.

clue.text: German and you heard too much (5)

indicators.note: only the sound of 'you' is wanted, not its spelling

blocks.note: und is German for 'and'
UE said after UND makes the 'yoo' sound

explanation.surface: A German speaker and you overheard something excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German and you' reads as two people; 'German and' is the German word for 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: Undue means excessive, more than is warranted: too much.

clue.text: Tidy chap fiddled with a misplaced pair of pictures (7)

indicators.note: fiddling with the letters rearranges them
the A has gone missing from the letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder
the A of CHAP is removed before rearranging

explanation.surface: A neat man has been meddling with two paintings, and lost one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misplaced' means lost here, not moved: the A leaves the fodder entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: A diptych is a work made of two painted or carved panels, often hinged together.

clue.text: Incomplete ballot is read differently in opposing camps (9)

indicators.note: POLL loses its last letter
IS READ is arranged differently

blocks.note: a poll is a ballot; incomplete drops the last L
anagram of IS READ

explanation.surface: A spoiled ballot paper is interpreted differently by the two sides.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an election count, where a half-filled ballot gets argued over by both camps.
explanation.definitionFit: A polarised electorate is split into two opposing camps.

clue.text: Small hand warmer in beau’s grip? (7)

blocks.note: S = small
a mitten keeps the hand warm

explanation.surface: A little glove warms a hand being held by a boyfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a mitten inside a beau's grip; the definition means in love, held by a beau's charms.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone smitten is infatuated, in the grip of love for a beau.

clue.text: Attractive body sheriff sometimes employs ironing trousers (13)

indicators.note: as a verb, to trouser is to pocket, so PRESSING takes POSSE inside it

blocks.note: pressing clothes is ironing them
a posse is the band a Wild West sheriff raises; it goes in after PRE

explanation.surface: A handsome sheriff's deputy is employed to iron trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like the garment being ironed; it is the verb, British slang for pocketing.
explanation.definitionFit: Prepossessing means attractive, making a good first impression.

clue.text: Recalled seeing that 50 per cent of girls dance (5)

indicators.note: called back, so the letters run backwards, upward in this down entry
fifty per cent is a half, so only half the letters of LASSES are kept: its first three

blocks.note: as = seeing that, since
the first half of LASSES; the whole string is then read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone remembers watching half the girls dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' reads as remembered, but it means called back, turned round. Lass is a Northern British word for girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: salsa, the Latin American dance from Cuban son and mambo, is one kind of dance.

clue.text: Legal statement bound back-to-front? (4)

indicators.note: the back letter comes to the front

blocks.note: to bound is to leap

explanation.surface: A legal statement that has been bound up in the wrong order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back-to-front' usually means reverse the whole word, which would give PAEL; here only the back letter comes to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea is a defendant's formal statement in court, such as guilty or not guilty.

clue.text: Trees come down on meadow, one after another (9)

blocks.note: a ley (or lea) is a meadow
to land is to come down, placed on LEY
I = one, twice in a row

explanation.surface: Trees fall one after another onto a meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: Leylandii are the fast-growing cypress hedges of British suburbs, famous for causing feuds between neighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Leyland cypress, a fast-growing conifer hybrid, is one kind of tree, and the Latin plural makes it trees.

clue.text: Long day interminable if unoccupied (3)

indicators.note: an unoccupied word has had everything inside it cleared out, leaving only its first and last letters

blocks.note: D = day
outer letters of INTERMINABLE

explanation.surface: A long day seems endless when there is nothing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' is the verb, as in 'dying to' or 'dying for' something. The surface is a dull empty day that never ends.
explanation.definitionFit: To die for something, informally, is to long for it badly.

clue.text: Spinner running through tail at Headingley (5)

indicators.note: the answer runs through the words, across the gap between them

blocks.note: hidden in taiL AT HEadingley

explanation.surface: A spin bowler runs through the tail of the batting order at a cricket ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Headingley is a Test cricket ground in Leeds, and a spinner running through the tail is a slow bowler taking the last batsmen's wickets. Here the spinner is a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A lathe spins wood or metal so it can be shaped.

clue.text: American always on X, man of accomplishment? (8)

blocks.note: A = American
chi is the Greek letter written X
ever = always, placed on CHI

explanation.surface: An American who is always posting on X is apparently a man of great accomplishment.
explanation.walkthrough: X suggests the social network or a kiss; it is the Greek letter chi.
explanation.definitionFit: An achiever is someone who accomplishes things; the question mark admits it need not be a man.

clue.text: Almost nobody on vessel for preserving Nelson’s arm? (6)

indicators.note: NONE falls one letter short

blocks.note: food is preserved in a can
NONE without its last letter, placed on CAN

explanation.surface: Pickling Admiral Nelson's lost arm in a jar.
explanation.walkthrough: Nelson lost his right arm in battle, and his body was famously preserved in brandy after Trafalgar; but his arm here is a weapon, a naval cannon.
explanation.definitionFit: A cannon was the main arm, or weapon, of Nelson's warships.
